cards.title: The central Sahel got wetter, 2000-2025
cards.headline: Across 48 one-degree land tiles (about 567,000 km²), GLDAS-2.1 precipitation shows a detectable wetting trend of +48.5% per decade (+3.52 mm/month per decade, median tile, 2000-2025). 100% of tiles are significant after false-discovery correction.

robustness.detail: Selection criterion (regions are built from these tiles, so this passes by design): 48 of 48 tiles (100%) significant with the matching sign after Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery correction (q < 0.05).

Median trend over 48 tiles (straight-line fit to annual means), in overlapping windows: 2000-2025 +48.4%/decade; 2003-2025 +50.0%/decade; 2000-2020 +37.5%/decade. Same sign, within a factor of 2. Global shares of significant land shrink in these windows (2003-2025: 1.3% wetting / 2.6% drying; 2000-2020: 0.7% wetting / 1.0% drying), but this region's trend keeps its sign and size.

robustness.check: Agreement between neighbour definitions (queen vs kNN LISA)
robustness.detail: With touching tiles as neighbours (queen contiguity), the local cluster test (LISA) labels 100% of tiles HH (a cluster of wetting trends). With the nearest tiles as neighbours (kNN), it labels 100% HH, and 100% of the queen HH tiles keep their label under kNN.

robustness.check: Agreement with an independent precipitation product (CHIRPS, via NASA FLDAS)
robustness.detail: Over 2003-2024, CHIRPS-based precipitation shows wetting in 100% of the 48 region tiles with FLDAS data (65% individually significant at p < 0.05); median trend +1.0 mm/month per decade vs +3.6 in GLDAS over the same years.
1 source, which agrees.

user.who: An agricultural extension office in the central Sahel (e.g. a district extension team in Chad)
user.decision: Which millet and sorghum varieties and sowing windows to recommend to smallholders for the coming rainy season
user.why_it_matters: Advice built on the drought decades of the 1970s-80s may now be too conservative. A detectable wetting trend supports testing longer-cycle varieties, but rainfall still varies from year to year, so recommendations should hedge against drought.

cards.evidence_level: strong pattern: passes all 4 extra checks (time windows, neighbours, second rainfall record, literature)

literature.citation: Biasutti, M. (2019). Rainfall trends in the African Sahel: Characteristics, processes, and causes. WIREs Climate Change, 10(4), e591.
literature.note: Reviews the partial recovery of Sahel rainfall since the 1980s drought, stronger in the central/eastern Sahel.

caveats: Percent changes look large in arid places because the baseline is small; read the mm/month figure alongside the percentage.
Sahel rainfall recovery is partial and uneven; the western Sahel has recovered less than the centre.
A wetter seasonal total can co-occur with more intense, less frequent storms; totals alone do not describe planting risk.
GLDAS-2.1 precipitation is model forcing (the weather data fed into the model) derived from GPCP; it is not an independent rain-gauge record.
Trends are statistical estimates over 2000-2025 and do not identify causes; the share of land with detectable trends shrinks in shorter windows, and individual trends can weaken.
Tile shares are after false-discovery correction; individual tiles can still be false positives.

cards.title: Paradox Earth caught a false trend
cards.headline: The apparent GLDAS-2.1 soil-water decline was withdrawn because it lines up with documented changes in the radiation data fed into the model (level shifts around 2010-08 and 2024-07) and disappears in a NASA land model with no such change in its input data (FLDAS, 2003-2024: +5.0 mm/decade, p = 0.14, no detectable trend).

robustness.detail: Soil water was the original headline, showing a 26-year global decline. Paradox Earth's own checks showed it is mostly two sudden level shifts that follow documented changes in the radiation data fed into the GLDAS model (a step in 2010-08 and a degraded period from 2024-07; GES DISC README_GLDAS2). Within the single consistent period 2012-01 to 2024-06 the global decline is not significant, so the trend was withdrawn and soil water is analysed only inside that window. README_GLDAS2 documents two problems in the model's radiation inputs (AGRMET/WWMCA): an apparent shift in the AGRMET climatology (section 1.5.3) and degraded WWMCA radiation from mid-2024 (section 1.2.3). The detected steps line up with both.

GLDAS-2.1 vs GLDAS-2.0: same Noah model and grid, different forcing, 2000-2014. At 2010-08 incoming solar radiation in the 2.1 forcing steps by +8.8 W/m² (95% CI +6.0 to +11.5); in 2.0 the step is -1.1 W/m² (95% CI -2.7 to +0.4). Evaporation responds only in 2.1. The 2011-2013 soil-water dip appears in both versions, deeper in 2.1, so the forcing change exaggerated a real dip into an apparent long-term decline. Soil-water trend over 2000-2014: -6.2 mm/decade in 2.1 (p = 0.08) vs -3.5 in 2.0 (p = 0.31).

FLDAS (Noah driven by MERRA-2 + CHIRPS, no radiation-forcing switch): global land soil water +5.0 mm/decade (95% CI -1.6 to +11.6, p = 0.14). There is no detectable global trend, and no decline. After FDR correction 2.8% of land is detectably wetting and 0.7% drying.

JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO MASCON RL06.3Mv04 CRI, 2003-2024: FDR-significant water-storage trends over 40% of land. GRACE weighs all water (groundwater, lakes, ice), so it cannot confirm or refute a soil-only trend. Where either is significant, GRACE and FLDAS soil water agree in sign over 61% of the area (Spearman 0.26). The largest GRACE declines are groundwater and irrigation hotspots the land model does not represent (NW India GRACE -204 vs model +34 mm/decade; North China Plain GRACE -108 vs model +9 mm/decade; California Central Valley GRACE -108 vs model -4 mm/decade).

user.who: Teachers and students using the Paradox Earth explorer
user.decision: Whether to trust a dramatic trend line before checking how the data were made
user.why_it_matters: Check a trend's input data for breaks before trusting its p-value; this apparent decline lines up with a change in the model's radiation forcing.

cards.evidence_level: withdrawn (data artefact caught by the detector's own checks)

literature.citation: NASA GES DISC. README Document for NASA GLDAS Version 2 Data Products (GLDAS-2.1 forcing section).
literature.note: States that the bias-correction scaling 'is unable to correct an apparent shift (of unknown origin) in the AGRMET climatology after 2011' for the radiation forcing.

literature.citation: Rodell, M., Houser, P. R., Jambor, U., et al. (2004). The Global Land Data Assimilation System. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 85(3), 381-394.
literature.note: Describes GLDAS as a model driven by changing observation-based forcing, which is why its outputs need homogeneity checks before trend analysis.

literature.citation: Qin, T., Feng, J., Zhang, X., Li, C., Fan, J., Zhang, C., Dong, B., Wang, H., & Yan, D. (2023). Continued decline of global soil moisture content, with obvious soil stratification and regional difference. Science of the Total Environment, 864, 160982.
literature.note: Reports a GLDAS-Noah soil-moisture decline (0-200 cm, 2000-2020); our checks attribute the post-2010 part largely to forcing changes. They analyse the model record as given; we test it for forcing breaks first.

caveats: The GLDAS-2.1 soil-water series is withdrawn as a trend and shown only as an example of a data artefact.
The 2011-2013 dip itself appears in both GLDAS versions, so it is likely a real dry spell; only the long-term decline is withdrawn.
FLDAS and GLDAS share the Noah land model, so FLDAS is independent in forcing, not in model physics.
Precipitation (the variable we do report) comes from GPCP-based forcing and is checked for the same kind of break and against CHIRPS.

cards.title: GRACE sees water loss the land model misses
cards.place: Northwest India and eastern Pakistan (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan; GRACE hotspot box 24-34°N, 68-80°E)
cards.headline: Over 2003-2024, GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite gravity shows water storage over northwest India falling by about 204 mm per decade (mean of 12 boxes, each 3° across; 8 are significant after false-discovery correction), while NASA's FLDAS land model, which has no groundwater pumping, shows soil water changing by +34 mm per decade. The missing water lines up with the groundwater depletion reported for this region in the literature.

robustness.detail: 8 of 12 boxes (67%), each 3° across, have GRACE/GRACE-FO water-storage trends that are significant after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, 2003-2024; all 8 are declines, and all 8 lie in the glacier-influenced zone (High Mountain Asia), so part of their signal may be glacier mass loss leaking into the GRACE grid cells (mascons) rather than groundwater. Not significant: 4 boxes, centred at 25.5°N.

robustness.check: Disagreement with the land model (NASA FLDAS soil water)
robustness.detail: Box mean: GRACE -204 mm/decade vs NASA FLDAS soil water (0-200 cm) +34 mm/decade. The signs are opposite. The land model has no groundwater pumping or irrigation and shows a rise in 12 of 12 boxes (0 FDR-significant). When GRACE sees a decline the land model does not, the gap points to storage the model does not track (groundwater, or glacier ice near the Himalaya). Globally, GRACE and FLDAS soil water agree in sign over 61% of the area where either is significant.
2 sources: 2 agree, 0 partly agree, 0 disagree.

robustness.check: Second GRACE solution (e.g. CSR or GSFC mascons)
robustness.detail: Only the JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO MASCON RL06.3Mv04 CRI solution was analysed.

user.who: A groundwater regulator or irrigation planner in Punjab-Haryana (e.g. a state groundwater authority)
user.decision: Whether to set or tighten groundwater extraction limits and crop-diversification incentives for over-exploited blocks
user.why_it_matters: Soil-moisture and rainfall products can look normal or even wet here while the aquifer is drawn down; GRACE measures total water storage, aquifer included, so it can catch a decline those products miss.

cards.evidence_level: observed (satellite gravity); cause not identified by this analysis

literature.citation: Rodell, M., Velicogna, I., & Famiglietti, J. S. (2009). Satellite-based estimates of groundwater depletion in India. Nature, 460, 999-1002.
literature.note: GRACE-based groundwater depletion over Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana (incl. Delhi), 2002-2008, attributed there to irrigation pumping.

literature.citation: Rodell, M., Famiglietti, J. S., Wiese, D. N., Reager, J. T., Beaudoing, H. K., Landerer, F. W., & Lo, M.-H. (2018). Emerging trends in global freshwater availability. Nature, 557, 651-659.
literature.note: Global GRACE trends 2002-2016; lists northern India among the largest water-storage declines, linked there to groundwater withdrawal.

caveats: GRACE mascons are a few hundred kilometres across; the box mean mixes irrigated plains with desert and foothills.
The northern boxes border the Himalaya; glacier mass loss can leak into them, so not all of the decline need be groundwater.
GRACE measures all water storage (groundwater, surface water, soil, snow and ice); this analysis does not separate them, and the cause is taken from the literature, not tested here.
Only one GRACE solution (JPL mascons) was analysed.

source.grace_product: JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO MASCON RL06.3Mv04 CRI
